### Reviewer 1

The authors make a compelling case for primary CD8 T-cells as sensitised for (RIPK1 induced) programmed cell death as instigators for triggering an elevated inflammatory response of autologous monocytes in patients with inherited inborn errors of cell death. Patient data (of 2 siblings) and mouse model data piece together a story that includes genetic reconstitution data, additional CRIA patient family data and is confirmed by anti-TNF/IFN treatment data of the patients. This reviewer is overall satisfied by the wealth of data presented. However, could it be that other cells, non-immune cells such as smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells and fibroblasts that can produce TNF, contribute to the auto inflammatory disease? It might not only CD8+ T-cells that instigate the cascade; perhaps TNF produced by tissue cells (non-immune cells) triggers the auto inflammatory cascade that otherwise works via increased sensitisation to apoptosis. please comment. Otherwise, only small points, a graphic summary would be a helpful addition to the manuscript (although the journal editors should decide if this fits). Two typographical errors seen in line 293 (generated) and 357 (specially).

### Reviewer 2

Dai et al have identified two related autoinflammatory disease patients with heterozygous variants in RIPK1 K377E/R390G. They associate these heterozygous variants with increased CD8+ T cell death and elevated inflammatory cytokine secretion from patient monocytes and macrophages. Disruption of crosstalk between CD8+ T cells and myeloid cells by pharmacological inhibition of TNF and JAK1/2 resulted in disease control. This is a noteworthy study which would be of interest to the rare disease community. The characterisation of individual cell types (T cells, monocytes, etc), their interactions and the proposed mechanism of how this drives disease is extensive and well executed, particularly use of the transwell culture system and HSCs-transplantation in Figure 5. However, the mechanistic insight into how the R390G variant contributes to disease is lacking and a cause for concern. Because this is a study on a single kindred to convincingly show that this is a monogenic disorder the authors should correct the patient mutations in patient cells (eg: fibroblasts) using homology directed repair or prime editing. Then determine NFkB signalling and cell death responses to TNF stimulation. These isogenic cells would be ideal controls in all follow up experiments. Disruption of the ubiquitination site: K377 through a missense substitution to an E is understandably pathogenic, RIPK1 ubiquitination at K377 is required for stable TNFR induced NFkB activation rather than TNFR triggered cell death (PMID: 16603398, PMID: 16543241, PMID: 32999468). Over expression of K377E RIPK1 in HT-29 cells shows a convincing increased phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL and decrease in NFkB signalling, ubiquitination of and elevated cell death, in response to TNF stimulation (Ex Fig 2), although these should be quantified and the appropriate number of experimental replications (ie: at least three) should be performed. These data, coupled with the induction of elevated NFkB driven cytokines in serum of mice transplanted with K377E RIPK1 T cells (Figure 5) provide a solid argument for K377E RIPK1 driving disease. In contrast, R390G RIPK1 expression alone had a limited effect on RIPK1 and MLKL phosphorylation and NFKB signalling in response to TNF stimulation (Ex data 2i and g). This data is particularly unconvincing since it is representative of only two replicates. At a minimum these experiments should be performed three times and densitometry changes for relevant bands should be presented (eg: (p)p65 compared to p65, IkBa bands relative to zero time point of each cell line, etc). Similarly, the change in TNFa and IL-6 in mouse serum in R390G RIPK1 expressing CD8+ linage cells is modest compared to WT RIPK1 expressing cells and it appears that this experiment has only been performed once. R390G RIPK1 overexpression does associate with increased TNF induced cell death in HT-29s (Ex Fig 2e-f) and R390G RIPK1 ubiquitination does appear delayed in Ex Fig 2l). But the data presented to validate the author’s proposed mechanism of R390G driving dysfunction of RIPK1 via interrupting interaction with MIB2 (Ex Fig 2l-n) is not convincing. Ubiquitination of WT and R390G RIPK1 looks comparable to me in Ex Fig 2m and the change in MIB2 binding in minimal in Ex Fig 2n and could be explained by the slightly smaller pulled down FLAG band (again, quantification using densitometry would help with data interpretation). The authors also do not provide reasoning on how a change to a glycine at 390 would interrupt binding to MIB2. Overall, I am not convinced that R390G RIPK1is a disease driving variant in itself, it may instead be a disease modifying variant that is only pathogenic in the context of a driving variant such as K377E. eg: R390G RIPK1 could have decreased stability and is not/lowly expressed in patient cells (this may not be seen in an over expression system), therefore disease pathogenesis is driven almost entirely driven by K377E. I note that while the CADD score is high, alpha missense rates this amino acid change for R390G as “ambiguous”. I encourage the authors to better determine the effect of R390G to publish the most robust findings which clinicians may take advice from. Here are a few points the authors should address to determine the role of R390G RIPK1: 1. Stability of R390G RIPK1: Use the established HT-29 over expression system to perform a cycloheximide chase to compare stability of R390G RIPK1 with other RIPK1 variants. 2. Interaction with MIB2: Try titrating levels of RIPK1 variants and/or MIB2 in the over expression IP to clearly show a decreased interaction between MIB2 and R390G over a range of concentrations. Alternatively, try BioID or TurboID. 3. Determine if Ubiquitination of RIPK1 at 377 is altered: Given that in the patient cells RIPK1 Ub is altered post TNF stimulation but the R390G mutant looks comparable to WT (over expression) it may be that (if stable) R390G inhibits K377 ubiquitination but does not affect other Ub sites on RIPK1. Thus, the change in Ub could be masked in the over expression system. The authors should specifically determine if K377 Ub is altered, eg: using plasmid mutagenesis to isolate specific Ub sites on RIPK1 and compare WT to R390G or perform Ub site mapping by Mass Spec. 4. Could R390G disrupt RIPK1 interaction with proteins other than MIB2 which are important for recruitment to the TNFR1 cytoplasmic domain or ubiquitination eg: TRADD (PMID: 8612133), cIAPs (PMID: 25192652) this could be tested in the same over expression system as Ex Data Fig 2. 5. The authors should also determine if R390 effects: RIPK1 trafficking to the TNFR1 complex, confirmational changes that allow RIPK1 to interact with other proteins or alters dimerization. I recommend the authors also try testing the above with coexpression of R390G with WT or K377E RIPK1 as this may contribute to the phenotype. Discussion Points that should be included: The authors should contextualise their findings on the T cell/Mono Mac driven disease course in autoinflammatory disorders driven by RIPK1 variants with autoinflammatory diseases driven by OTULIN deficiency/dysfuncton(driven almost entirely by myeloid cells, PMID: 30804083) and LUBAC deficient patients (more involvement of lymphocytes and stromal cell types, eg: PMID: 32687504, PMID: 31462647, PMID: 35534698, etc) The equivocation of monoclonal blockade of IFNg in Figure 5f and treatment of patients with ruxolitinib (Fig 6) is incorrect, JAK1/2 blockade inhibits inflammatory signalling from a variety of cytokines including IFNab and IL-6 which are elevated in the RIPK1 patients. I appreciate that the authors call this treatment regime TNF/IFN but the distinction should be highlighted in the discussion. Particularly because RIPK1 has been shown to drive IFNab signalling under conditions of OTULIN dysfuncton(PMID: 29950720) and JAK1/2 blockade had therapeutic benefit in these patients (PMC11022884 ). Do the authors think that IFNg is specifically is important for cell death in these patients as per PMID: 35139355? -No increase in TSZ induced cell death compared to TS and TZ, in fact TSZ looked less effective than TS in T cells (Figure 1h) -comment? Minor Points: The manuscript presents an impressive amount of experimental data; but many key experiments have been performed only once or twice (from my reading of the legends) and generally only show a single representative repeat. As I highlighted in the context of western blotting of the NFkB signalling cascade this is a real problem when trying to establish the robustness of the patient phenotype. This is particularly important to the field of rare disease since these findings may be used for differential diagnosis of other patients, reporting that there is a strong effect when it is actually variable will impede our understanding of other novel RIPK1 variants. The authors need to repeat key experiments at least three times to strengthen the validity of their conclusions and provide summary data from independent biological replicates (ie: pooling results across experiments). -Ex Figure 2A is missing panels and does not appear to show protection from cell death by Nec-1 in patient fibroblasts. Please quantify to clearly show this result. -Ext Fig 3e, panels are missing -Extended 2d,e should have empty vector control -No isotype controls shown for Fig 2f -Please list for cytokine groups in Figure 3. “which was reported to induce more severer cell death in Ripk1K376R/K376R cells” Should say: “which was reported to induce more sever cell death …"

### Reviewer 3

Biallelic loss-of-functon(LOF) variants in RIPK1 cause RIPK1 deficiency, whereas monoallelic cleavage-resistant gain-of-functon(GOF) variants result in an autoinflammatory syndrome called cleavage-resistant RIPK1 induced autoinflammatory (CRIA) syndrome. In this manuscript, Jialin Dai, Qing Zhou, and colleagues describe two patients from a single family harboring compound heterozygous missense variants in RIPK1 (K377E and R390G), who presented with an autoinflammatory syndrome characterized by recurrent fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, and enteropathy. At the molecular level, the RIPK1-K377E variant was shown to be ubiquitination-deficient and constitutively active. The R390G variant is also considered a GOF mutation, although concerns remain regarding its pathogenicity and molecular mechanism, as discussed in major comment no. 4. Functional studies demonstrated augmented apoptosis and necroptosis following TNF stimulation in the patients’ dermal fibroblasts and primary T cells, consistent with RIPK1 GOF activity. scRNA-seq of patients’ PBMCs identified an aberrant monocyte/macrophage population with elevated proinflammatory cytokine expression. CyTOF-based PBMC subset analysis revealed reduced frequencies of CD8+ T cells in the patients. Upon anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation in in vitro, a further decrease in CD8-hi T cells and an emergence of CD8-lo T cells were noted. Cytokine production was enhanced in both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells. Co-culture experiments with patient-derived T cells and healthy donor monocyte-derived macrophages demonstrated that the patient T cells exacerbated proinflammatory cytokine production by allogeneic monocyte-derived macrophages, suggesting a central role of T cells in driving autoinflammation in these patients. Therapeutically, the patients’ autoinflammatory manifestations were successfully managed with the anti-TNFα monoclonal antibody adalimumab and the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib. Notably, a reduced proportion of CD8+ T cells among total T cells was also consistently observed in other immune dysregulation conditions, including CRIA and SHARPIN deficiency. In summary, the experiments in this study are thoughtfully designed, and the data generated are largely robust and support the central conclusions. However, several experiments require revision or clarification, as detailed in the major and minor comments below. This study demonstrate decreased CD8+ T cells as one of common immunological abnormalities in other inborn errors of cell death (IECD) such as CRIA and SHARPIN deficiency, indicating the CD8+ T cell-driven autoinflammation may play a role in other IECDs. While this study will likely be of interest to researchers in the field of inborn errors of immunity, the findings may limit its appeal to the broader readership of Nature Communications. I believe the manuscript may be more appropriately suited for a clinically oriented journal that emphasizes translational research and patient-centered findings. Major comments: 1. One of the study’s principal observations is the pronounced depletion of CD8+ T cells in patients carrying RIPK1‑K377E/R390G variants and, similarly, in those with CRIA. The authors hypothesize that augmented programmed cell death of CD8+ T cells results in increased cytokine release from those cells, in turn, potentiate monocytes and macrophages to secrete proinflammatory cytokines. To support this model, direct comparisons of CD8+ versus CD4+ T cell responses are indispensable. Several critical comparisons, however, are currently missing: - Viability following TS or TSZ stimulation (as shown in Fig 1h) for CD8+ versus CD4+ T cells - Phosphorylation of MLKL (as shown in Extended Data Fig 2c) in CD8+ versus CD4+ T cells - Proliferation following anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation (as shown in Fig 4b) for CD8+ versus CD4+ T cells 2. In Fig. 3g‑j, both RIPK1 phosphorylation and caspase‑3 cleavage appear more pronounced in CD4+ than in CD8+ T cells. This seems at odds with the model that positions CD8+ T cells as the primary drivers of the pathogenesis. Could the authors clarify this discrepancy? 3. In Fig 4e and 4f, Patient 2 already shows an expanded CD4/8 double‑negative T cell (DNT) population at baseline (day 0), and this subset appears to increase further over time. - Were elevated DNT frequencies observed consistently in all patients’ (P1 and P2) PBMC samples? - Are these DNTs αβ T cells or γδ T cells? If they are αβ DNTs, it is important to assess whether they originate from CD8+ T cells. Clarifying the identity and origin of the DNT compartment is critical, as it could significantly impact the interpretation of CD8+ T-cell reduction in these patients. To directly address this, CD8+ T cells should be isolated and stimulated under the same conditions used in Fig. 4f to determine whether they transition into the DNT phenotype. 4. Pathogenicity and underlying molecular mechanism of the RIPK1‑R390G variant are not yet convincingly demonstrated. Given that the monoallelic CRIA‑associated RIPK1 variants act as GOF alleles, the pathogenic potential of biallelic GOF variants must be interpreted with caution. Below are the reasons of my concern: - MLKL phosphorylation in R390G‑transduced HT‑29 cells is markedly lower than in K377E (Extended Data Fig 2g). - pIKKα/β ,pp65, pIκBα, pERK, and pJNK in R390G-transduced HT-29 cells following TNF stimulation seem almost comparable to WT (Extended Data Fig 2i). - Despite a modestly reduced MIB2 interaction (Extended Data Fig 2n), total ubiquitination of R390G RIPK1 appears intact (Extended Data Figs 2m) Extended Data Fig 2d also may indicate ubiquitination of RIPK1-R390G is normal (there was no apparent size difference between WT and R390G RIPK1, whereas the K377E variant exhibited a reduced molecular weight, which may reflect impaired ubiquitination). The statement in Line 167 (“The reduced interaction between MIB2 and R390G could partly explained the impaired ubiquitination of R390G RIPK1.”) therefore seems inaccurate. Taken together, the evidence still allows for the possibility of RIPK1-K377E being pathogenic GOF variant with incomplete penetrance, rather than the R390G being bona fide GOF variant. I would recommend following experiments to address this point. - Immunophenotyping of mono‑allelic K377E and R390G carriers to determine whether either (or both) variant(s) consistently segregates with immunological abnormalities such as increased CD4/8 ratio. - Assessment of RIPK1 ubiquitination in patient‑derived cells or in K377E/R390G double knock‑in cell lines. 5. Interpretation of scRNAseq analysis requires revision. The manuscript does not describe the methodology used to assign hematopoietic cell subset identities to the identified clusters. Please describe the tool/reference used for cell type assignment in the Methods section. The UMAP illustrates cell types that are either rare or absent in peripheral blood such as an oversized NKT cluster and a megakaryocyte cluster. With such data, it is inaccurate to discuss the quantitative assessment of the specific population (Line 176: The monocyte compartment in patients was significant expanded (Fig. 2a, Extended Data Fig. 3a). The CyTOF data do not show an expanded monocyte compartment. Did the patients’ complete blood counts (CBCs) reveal monocytosis? Moreover, the expanded cluster in the scRNA‑seq analysis is labelled “LDG,” not CD14+ or CD16+ monocytes. A more rational model would be that the cluster unique to patients, currently labelled “LDG”, represents a pathogenic, cytokine‑high monocyte subset. Intracellular staining of IL-1β and IL-6 show a bimodal distribution within the monocyte (Fig. 2f), indicating two functionally distinct subsets. 6. The current title is too broad. Consider rephrasing it to reflect the key discoveries. Minor comments: 1. Line 98: Please clarify whether the perianal abscess was of infectious origin or a manifestation of autoinflammation. If it was infectious, the phrasing in lines 103–104 may need to be revised accordingly. 2. Line 106: Do the authors have any insights into the cause of elevated ADA levels observed in the patients? 3. Line 135 / Fig 1h: Although the manuscript states that T cells from heterozygous carriers and controls did not exhibit sensitivity to TS/TSZ stimulation, both the father and mother appear to show an intermediate phenotype. This should be confirmed by repeating the experiment in the parental samples and expanding the number of healthy controls. 4. Line 131 / Extended Data Fig 2a: Some data in Extended Data Fig 2a are lacking and difficult to interpret. However, the available data ( TS vs TS + Nec-1s in P2) do not clearly support the manuscript’s claim that Nec-1s rescued both apoptosis and necroptosis in patient-derived HDFs. Please clarify or revise this point. 5. Line 163: The list of E3 ubiquitin ligases that were screened should be stated, even if the data are not shown. 6. Line 167: Reference 20 does not provide evidence of MIB2-mediated RIPK1 ubiquitination. Please ensure that citations accurately reflect the claims being made. 7. ## Paper

## Abstract

Systemic autoinflammatory diseases (SAID) with inborn errors of cell death (IECD) are caused by overactivation of programmed cell death (PCD). However, the pathogenesis by which PCD leads to autoinflammation remains unclear. Here, we identified IECD patients carrying compound heterozygous RIPK1 variants K377E/R390G with autoinflammatory manifestations. Mechanistically, K377E and R390G mutations suppress NF-κB signaling and activate RIPK1 to promote cell death. CD8+ T cells of the patients displayed overactivated RIPK1 and excessive cell death, leading to an elevated CD4/CD8 ratio, which could also be detected in patients with cleavage-resistant mutation of RIPK1 or SHARPIN deficiency. We show that the increased cell death of CD8+ T cells promotes TNF and IFN-γ secretion to activate monocytes/macrophages, which triggers overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines. In addition, disruption of the communication between T cells and monocytes/macrophages through pharmacologic blockade of TNF and IFN attenuates proinflammatory cytokine production in macrophages and relieves all the symptoms in patients. This study further clarifies the mechanism for a group of IECD with SAID. Increased CD4/CD8 ratio and augmented RIPK1 activation in T cells provide potentially additional criteria for diagnosis of RIPK1-dependent IECD and a combination of TNF/JAK inhibitor could be an effective therapy for the diagnosed patients.

---

## Introduction

Systemic autoinflammatory diseases (SAIDs) are a group of disorders induced by overactivation of the innate immune system characterized by recurrent fever and multi-organ inflammation, but typically without high-titer antibodies or antigen-specific T cells1, 2. To date, more than 50 genes responsible for monogenic SAIDs have been identified. The list of genes whose mutations lead to SAIDs is enriched with key regulators of programmed cell death (PCD). Enhanced PCD is one of the characteristics in the SAID patients caused by the cleavage resistance mutations in RIPK13, 4, 5 or deficiencies of RIPK16, 7, TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) 8, OTU deubiquitinase with linear linkage specificity (OTULIN), HOIL1-interacting protein (HOIP) 9, Heme-oxidized IRP2 ubiquitin ligase-1 (HOIL1) 10, and Shank-associated RH domain-interacting protein (SHARPIN) 11. This clinical entity is designated as ‘inborn errors of cell death (IECD)’ 11. Pathogenic variants of IECD have been shown to activate apoptosis and necroptosis in cellular or murine models12. Therapies targeting inflammatory cytokines, such as anti-IL6, anti-TNF, or anti-IL-1 antibodies, were applied to treat IECD patients, but refractory cases still showed unresponsiveness or tolerance after long-term treatment3, 5, 8, 11. Therefore, investigation of therapies targeting upstream molecules is urgently needed to offer more effective treatment on the refractory SAID with IECD.

The excessive cell death is strongly linked to autoinflammatory diseases in humans, while the pathogenesis by which cell death causes spontaneous inflammation in these conditions is unknown. The study of the pathogenesis aids the improvement of targeted therapy for refractory IECD.

RIPK1 is a key mediator of cell death and inflammation13. Overactivation of RIPK1 leads to enhanced apoptosis, necroptosis, and inflammatory response in mice and humans14. Whereas RIPK1 deficiency and heterozygous non-cleavable variants in RIPK1 cause immunodeficiency and dominantly inherited autoinflammatory diseases, respectively, a recessive autoinflammatory disease caused by RIPK1 variants has not been reported. K63-linked ubiquitination of RIPK1 on K377 is essential for NF-κB pathway activation and negative regulation of cell death. Mice bearing Ripk1K376R/K376R knockin mutation display embryonic lethality due to excessive apoptosis and necroptosis caused by RIPK1 activation15, 16, 17. Nevertheless, the function of RIPK1 ubiquitination in human disease has not been defined or studied. In this study, we identified two autoinflammatory patients carrying recessively inherited compound heterozygous RIPK1 variants K377E/R390G. We demonstrate that RIPK1 K377E/R390G variants lead to autoinflammatory disease by promoting RIPK1 activation-mediated death of CD8+ T cells and identify TNF and IFN-γ as molecules linking programmed cell death and autoinflammation.

---

## Results

Biallelic RIPK1 mutations in patients with autoinflammation

We identified two children from one family with autoinflammatory disease characterized by recurrent fevers, lymphadenopathy, and skin rashes (Fig. 1a-d). They also developed colitis characterized by diarrhea, abdominal pain and perianal abscess. At the age of 7 months and 4 years, respectively, patient 1 (P1) and patient 2 (P2) displayed fever episodes that lasted 3-4 days and recurred every 8-9 days. Their fever episodes were accompanied by elevated serum C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid A (SAA), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), D-dimer, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Figure. 1a-c). Neither patient exhibited evidence of immunodeficiency. In addition, the levels of proinflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF were strongly increased in the serum of both patients during flares (Fig. 1f). Serum CRP levels and adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity in patients were higher than those of unaffected controls and parents during disease flares and even in remission (Fig. 1f). P1 had taken prednisone during flares, with resolution of fever but limited effect on inflammatory indexes (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Figure. 1a-c).

By performing whole exome sequencing (WES) and Sanger sequencing on the family, we identified that both P1 and P2 carried the RIPK1 compound heterozygous mutations (c. 1129A>G / p. K377E and c. 1168C>G / p. R390G), whereas their unaffected mother (and maternal grandmother) and father (and paternal grandmother) were heterozygous carriers of RIPK1 R390G and K377E, respectively (Supplementary Figure. 1d, e). All heterozygous family members were healthy. Therefore, this autoinflammatory disease in the siblings is recessively inherited and segregated with the inheritance of both RIPK1 variants. The lysine residue at amino acid position 377 is the site for K63-linked ubiquitination of RIPK118, while the function of residue R390 has not been characterized. Both K377 and R390 residues are conserved in RIPK1 across species (Supplementary Figure. 1f). The two RIPK1 variants were predicted to be deleterious with their CADD scores well above that of the non-cleavable RIPK1 mutations D324V, D324H, and D324N (Supplementary Figure. 1g). No other candidate variants were identified by WES.

Given that RIPK1 is a widely expressed regulator of programmed cell death, we utilized SV40-immortalized human dermal fibroblasts (SV40-HDFs) and primary T cells derived from unaffected controls and P2 to assess the sensitivity to apoptosis induced by TNF (T) with cIAP1/2 degrader SM-164 (S) as well as necroptosis induced by TNF (T) with pan-caspase inhibitor z-VAD-FMK (Z) or TSZ. HDFs from P2 showed increased susceptibility to both TZ/TSZ-induced necroptosis, which was fully rescued by RIPK1 kinase inhibitor Necrostatin-1s (Nec-1s), and to TS-induced apoptosis, which was only partially inhibited by Nec-1s (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Figure. 2a). Primary T cells isolated from patients, but not heterozygous carriers and unaffected controls, were more sensitive to TS-induced apoptosis or TSZ-induced necroptosis, which was in accordance with the recessive inheritance pattern (Fig. 1h). P2’s SV40-HDFs and P1’s primary T cells displayed higher levels of RIPK1 phosphorylation at S166 and MLKL phosphorylation at S358 under cell death stimulation, and these patterns could be inhibited by Nec-1s (Supplementary Figure. 2b, c), indicating that SV40-HDFs and T cells bearing K377E/R390G mutations were prone to RIPK1 activation-induced cell death. Thus, compound R390G and K377E mutations in RIPK1 sensitized patients’ cells to programmed cell death.

To further investigate the function of K377E and R390G mutations in RIPK1 under isogenic conditions, we established HT-29 cell models with either the K377E or R390G knockin mutation. Both mutant cell lines showed increased sensitivity to TZ-induced cell death (Supplementary Figure. 2d). The elevated cell death levels, along with enhanced RIPK1 and MLKL phosphorylation in K377E and R390G knockin HT-29 cells, could be reversed by Nec-1s (Supplementary Figure. 2e, f). Thus, both K377E and R390G mutations in RIPK1 could promote cell death. We also determined the effect of RIPK1 K377E and R390G mutations on the TNFR1 downstream NF-κB and MAPK pathways. The activation of both NF-κB and ERK signaling was partially impaired in P2 HDFs compared to unaffected controls. Consistently, NF-κB activation and p38 phosphorylation were also suppressed in K377E or R390G knockin HT-29 cells upon TNF stimulation (Supplementary Figure. 2g, h). Consequently, the transcription of TNF, IL1B, and IL8 was reduced in K377E or R390G knockin HT-29 cells compared to WT control (Supplementary Figure. 2i). The TNFR signaling complex forms upon TNF stimulation is crucial for NF-κB activation 19. Notably, both P2 HDFs and K377E or R390G knockin HT-29 cells showed reduced RIPK1 ubiquitination shifts within the TNFR signaling complex (Supplementary Figure. 2j, k). K377 is a ubiquitination site in the RIPK1 intermediate domain (ID domain) 18. Consistently, the K377E mutation, but not R390G, directly abolished the ubiquitination of the ID domain (Supplementary Figure. 2l). Since R390 is not expected to be a direct site for ubiquitination, we considered the possibility that R390G might affect the recruitment of E3 ubiquitination modifiers. We screened key reported key regulators of K63-linked ubiquitination within the TNFR signaling complex, including the E3 ubiquitin ligases TNF Receptor-Associated Factor 2 (TRAF2), cellular Inhibitor of Apoptosis 1 (cIAP-1), cellular Inhibitor of Apoptosis 2 (cIAP-2), Mind Bomb-2 (MIB2), Tumor Necrosis Factor Alpha-Induced Protein 3 (A20), the deubiquitinase cylindromatosis (CYLD), as well as the key adaptor protein TRADD (TNFR1-associated death domain protein). We found that the interaction between MIB2 and the RIPK1 R390G mutation was significantly reduced (Supplementary Figure. 2m, n). Furthermore, MIB2 has been reported to mediate the ubiquitination of RIPK1 at Lys377 and Lys 63420. The reduced interaction between MIB2 and R390G therefore could explain the impaired ubiquitination of the R390G RIPK1 mutant. Collectively, these data demonstrate that both K377E and R390G mutations promote RIPK1 activation-dependent cell death and impair pro-survival NF-κB signaling.

Activation of inflammatory signaling in myeloid cells of the patients

We next studied the inflammatory signaling pathways by performing single-cell RNA sequencing on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from P1, P2, and unaffected controls. The myeloid compartment in patients was significantly expanded (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Figure. 3a). Similar to the previously reported RIPK1 D324V mutant4, transcriptional up-regulation of proinflammatory cytokines (IL1B and CXCL8) was detected in patient cells, especially in monocyte subsets (Fig. 2b). Likewise, differential gene expression analysis revealed the greatest up-regulation of genes governed by NF-κB and type-I IFN pathways in myeloid cells from the patients (Fig. 2c, d, Supplementary Figure. 3b, c). The up-regulated genes in the patients’ monocytes were also enriched for pathways of cytokine production, cytokine stimulation, and negative regulation of cell death in the gene ontology (GO) analysis (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Figure. 3d), suggesting that myeloid cells play a crucial role in increased cytokine production and proinflammatory signal transduction in the patients. Increased basal expression of IL-1β, IL-6 as well as IFNγ in monocytes from P1 was confirmed by flow cytometry (Fig. 2f). However, monocytes isolated from the patients exhibited reduced transcription of NF-κB regulated genes including IL1B, IL6, CXCL8 and TNF in response to TNF stimulation (Fig. 2g), in accordance with the partially suppressed NF-κB activation in SV40-HDFs as demonstrated earlier (Supplementary Figure. 2g). As RIPK1 overactivation can promote PCD-induced inflammation21, we hypothesized that excessive cell death in myeloid cells instead of impaired TNF-stimulated NF-κB and MAPK signaling, were the main cause of systemic inflammation.

Thus, we assessed the cell death response of monocytes to TNF stimulation. The monocytes from the patients were more sensitive to TS-induced apoptosis than that of unaffected controls, whereas they showed similar sensitivity to necroptosis induced by TSZ (Fig. 2h). In addition, no differences of apoptosis and necroptosis were observed between monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) from patients and that from unaffected controls (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Figure. 3e). On the other hand, although the expression of cell death suppressor genes, including TNFAIP3, BCL2A1, BCL6, BCL3, RNF144B, BIRC2 and BIRC3, was elevated across various patient immune cell types, their expression levels were markedly higher in myeloid lineage cells compared to lymphocyte subsets (Fig. 2j, k and Supplementary Figure. 3f). Therefore, the elevated inflammatory response of monocytes in patients may be regulated non-autonomously by other cell types that were more susceptible to cell death.

Myeloid cells and T cells play different roles in IECD patients

To identify the upstream factors driving the inflammatory cytokine production in myeloid cells, we performed a semi-quantitative protein microarray analysis on serum samples from unaffected controls and P2 (Fig. 3a, b). Samples from P2 were collected both before and after the first fever episode (disease onset). Differentially expressed cytokines compared to healthy donors were clustered into 3 groups based on their changing patterns relative to the fever stage. Group 1 comprised 26 cytokines (e.g., IL-1β) that peaked exclusively during the flare, indicating their specific association with the febrile stage (Fig. 3c, Supplementary Figure. 4a, b). Group 2 contained 24 cytokines (e.g., sCD95) that were persistently elevated, while Group 3 consisted of 32 cytokines that showed a continuous decrease (Fig. 3c, Supplementary Figure. 4c-f). The expression levels of cytokines in Groups 2 and 3 were consistently altered, suggesting they were likely directly influenced by the genetic mutations rather than being secondary to the fever episodes.

In order to further define the source of the cytokines in group 1 and 2, we compare the expression scores of the two groups between patients and unaffected controls by analyzing single-cell RNA-seq data. The cytokines in group 1 were most significantly up-regulated in patients’ monocytes, low-density granulocyte (LDG), plasmacytoid dendritic cell (pDC), and plasma cells (Fig. 3d), consistent with the strong inflammatory signature in myeloid cells during fever. Thus, amplification of inflammation by myeloid cells is an important step for fever episode. Notably, the genes encoding cytokines in group 2 were up-regulated most significantly in the patients’ lymphocyte subsets, especially in CD8+ T cells, implying a pathogenic role of K377E/R390G variants in T lymphocytes (Fig. 3e, Supplementary Figure. 4g). In addition, the expression levels of cell death suppressor genes in T lymphocytes were also lower compared with myeloid cells (Supplementary Figure. 3f), suggesting that T lymphocytes may be sensitized to undergo programmed cell death. These results supported a critical role of monocytes in promoting inflammation and implied that T lymphocyte subsets may also contribute to the pathophysiology of this autoinflammatory disease.

RIPK1 activation leads to increased PCD and CD4/CD8 ratio in T cells

To better understand the impact of RIPK1 mutations on the immune profile, we performed cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) on PBMCs isolated from unaffected controls and patients. CyTOF result revealed that CD4+ T, B, and γδ T cell proportions in patients were elevated, whereas CD8+ T and NK cell proportions were reduced compared to unaffected controls (Supplementary Figure. 5a, b). Apoptosis, indicated by cleaved caspase-3, was increased in CD8+ TEMRA, γδT, NK, and B cell subsets of patients (Fig. 3f). Flow cytometric analysis confirmed that patients’ CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, not CD19+ B cells and CD14+ monocytes, displayed augmented activation of RIPK1 and cleaved caspase-3 (Fig. 3g-j and Supplementary Figure. 5c-5g). Therefore, T cells were the most sensitive compartment for RIPK1 activation and PCD in vivo.

The CyTOF results also revealed a global activation of patients’ immune cells as indicated by CD69 expression, while elevated CD38 expression appeared to be restricted to B cells and T cells (Supplementary Figure. 5h, i). Increased expression of CD69 in T cells was further validated by flow cytometry (Fig. 3k). Concomitantly, higher levels of T cell activation-related proinflammatory mediators, including sCD25, TNF, and IFNγ, were observed in the serum of P1 and P2 as well as (cleavage-resistant RIPK1-induced autoinflammatory) CRIA patients (Fig. 3l), indicating that patients' T cells were overactivated.

Activated lymphocytes undergo cell expansion and indeed we observed an elevation in the number of total lymphocytes, as well as that of CD3+ T cells, CD4+ T cells and B cells, except for that of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NKT cells in the immunophenotyping results (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Figure. 6a). As a consequence of the loss of CD8+ T cells, CD4/CD8 ratio was significantly increased in patients. Of note, CD4/CD8 T cell ratio in heterozygous parents remained normal, indicating that alteration of this ratio requires biallelic K377/R390 variants in RIPK1 (Supplementary Figure. 6b). In vitro expansion of T cells isolated from P1 upon anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation was abnormal, but the proliferation ability was undampened (Fig. 4b, c), reflecting the occurrence of T cell death. Specifically, CD8+ T cells went through a contraction phase after activation, presumably resulted from activation-induced cell death (AICD) 22. The augmented signal of CD95 (Fas) on the surface of patients’ T cells, accompanied by elevations of serum sCD95 and CD95L levels, also supported increased AICD (Fig. 4d).

To further characterize the abnormalities in the patient's T cells, we analyzed T cell subsets from in vitro cultured PBMCs. We observed that CD8 expression was decreased in approximate half of the CD8+ T cells after culturing PBMCs isolated from P2 in vitro for 24 hours, while the expression on CD8+ T cells of unaffected controls remained normal (Fig. 4e). Through gating on CD8hi (CD8+ T cells with normal CD8 expression) or CD8lo (CD8+ T cells with lower CD8 expression) T cells, we found that in contrast to CD8hi T cells, most of the CD8lo T cells exhibited augmented cleaved caspase-3, indicative of activated apoptosis. In addition, total RIPK1 level in CD8lo T cells decreased, which may be caused by caspase-3 cleavage (Fig. 4e).

The decreased CD8 expression in patients’ T cells and the increases in CD4/CD8 ratio were more prominent after prolonged in vitro culture or after TS or TSZ stimulation compared to that of control (Fig. 4f, Supplementary Figure. 6c-e). Therefore, we hypothesized that CD8+ T cells were more prone to undergo PCD than CD4+ T cells. Then we isolated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from patients and heterozygous carriers and stimulated with TS or TSZ. We found that CD8+ T cells were more sensitive to PCD than CD4+ T cells, which explained the increase of the CD4/CD8 ratio under PCD stimulation (Supplementary Figure. 6f, g). Moreover, we also performed in situ knock-in of WT RIPK1 in patients’ T cells, which successfully reversed the CD4/CD8 ratio induced by TS or TSZ, further confirming the activated RIPK1 resulting in increased cell death and CD4/CD8 ratio in T cells (Fig. 4g, h and Supplementary Figure. 6h, i). In contrast, neither ferroptosis induced by RSL3 nor RIPK1-independent apoptosis induced by staurosporine (STS) can differentiate cell death of CD8+ T cells from the patients compared to that of unaffected controls (Supplementary Figure. 6j). In addition, the activation of patients’ T cells by anti-CD3 antibody stimulation increased CD4/CD8 ratio, which could be reversed by ponatinib or partially reversed by Nec-1s (Fig. 4i, j and Supplementary Figure. 6k, l). Since ponatinib inhibits the kinase activity of RIPK1 and RIPK3 23, these results suggest that they might play important roles in regulating AICD in the patient T cells bearing K377E/R390G compound RIPK1 mutations.

To investigate the effect of RIPK1 K377E and R390G mutations on the CD4/CD8 ratio of T cells in mice, we crossed Ripk1K376R/+ with Ripk1+/– mice to generate Ripk1K376R/− mice, which could be weaned at Mendelian ratio but develop severe systemic inflammation (Supplementary Figure. 6m) 15, 16. Interestingly, no difference of CD4/CD8 ratio in peripheral T cells was observed between Ripk1K376R/– and Ripk1+/– mice at 3 weeks old (Fig. 4k). In contrast, the CD4/CD8 ratio in peripheral T cells from 8-week-old Ripk1K376R/− mice was significantly higher than that in the other three genotypes (Fig. 4l, Supplementary Figure. 6n), which is consistent with that of K377E/R390G patients. Together, these results suggested that T cells, especially CD8+ T cells, were the most susceptible hematopoietic lineage to RIPK1 activation-induced cell death, as reflected by the elevated CD4/CD8 in patients with the RIPK1 K377E/R390G variants.

RIPK1 activation-induced T cell death drives inflammation in myeloid cells

Given the differential impact of the RIPK1 K377E/R390G variants on T cells and myeloid cells, we next investigated cell-cell communication between these two cell types using a transwell system (Fig. 5a). The results showed that patients’ T cells induced higher cytokine expression in monocytes derived macrophages (MDMs) comparing to that of T cells isolated from unaffected controls (Fig. 5b, c). However, MDMs from patients showed less response than that of unaffected controls upon culturing with the identical T cells. The impaired inflammatory response by patients’ MDMs may be explained by the suppressed NF-κB activation caused by RIPK1 K377E/R390G mutations. Interestingly, patients’ T cells could still trigger massive cytokine production in autologous MDMs (Supplementary Figure. 7a). Thus, we conclude that T cells from the patients can act to potentiate the inflammatory response of monocytes and macrophages with RIPK1 K377E/R390G mutations.

Previous studies have proposed TNF and IFNγ secreted by chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells as key contributors to the activation of macrophages during cytokine release syndrome (CRS) 24. TNF combined with IFNγ was also reported to be a key inducer of inflammation in patients with severe COVID-19 25. IFNγ and TNF were specifically upregulated in patients’ T lymphocytes and NK cells, whereas receptors of these two cytokines were highly expressed in myeloid cells (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Figure. 7b, c), providing additional support for T cell-monocyte/macrophage communication through these two receptor-ligand pairs. In comparison to unaffected controls, T cells, especially CD8+ T cells from patients, exhibited greater production of IFNγ and TNF. The production of these cytokines was further enhanced upon TS or TSZ stimulation (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Figure. 7d). These results indicated that IFNγ and TNF produced by activated T cells may be the key factors to initiate the inflammatory response of MDMs. Consistently, increased production of TNF, IL1B, and IL6 in MDMs generated from unaffected controls stimulated by either patient T cells or anti-CD3/CD28-activated donor-matched T cells could be partially inhibited by neutralization of IFNγ or TNF alone. The cytokine production was completely blocked by combined blockade of IFNγ and TNF (Fig. 5f, Supplementary Figure. 7e). Collectively, these data demonstrated that RIPK1 overactivation in CD8+ T cells promote TNF and IFNγ secretion to trigger inflammatory cytokine production in MDMs.

In order to validate this model and assess whether the function of RIPK1 K377E and R390G mutations in CD8+ T cells was sufficient to induce inflammation, we exploited the Cre-loxp system combined with bone marrow transplantation to conditionally express WT or mutated human RIPK1 in specific hematopoietic compartments (Fig. 5g, Supplementary Figure. 8a). Mouse lineage negative bone marrow cells (Lin- BMs, including hematopoietic stem cells and marrow stromal cells) isolated from donor Cd8-creERT2 mice or Lyz2-creERT2 mice were transduced with lentivirus encoding EF1α-promoted loxp-GFP-stop-loxp-TagBFP2-P2A-human RIPK1 expression cassettes (LSL-hRIPK1). Afterwards, transduced Line- BMs were transplanted into lethally irradiated donor mice followed by tamoxifen induction. Transplantation efficiency and the specificities of Cd8 and Lyz2 promoters were validated (Supplementary Figure. 8b-h). GFP expression in Line- BMs reflected transduction efficiency, and TagBFP2 confirmed WT/mutated RIPK1 expression in specific cell types upon tamoxifen induction (Supplementary Figure. 9). We then evaluated the serum levels of inflammatory cytokines in the recipients. Under basal conditions, serum Tnf and Il-6 levels were higher in mice with CD8+ T cells expressing mutated RIPK1 (K377E, R390G or D324V) than WT RIPK1 and empty vector (EV) controls (Fig. 5h). No significant differences were observed between mice bearing myeloid cells overexpressing EV/WT RIPK1 controls and mutated RIPK1 (Fig. 5i). The result demonstrated the pathogenic function of K377E and R390G as well as the initiator role of T cells in the autoinflammation.

Combined therapy targeting TNF and IFNγ reverses systemic inflammation in the patients

Since TNF and IFNγ were considered to mediate the inflammatory cytokine production of myeloid cells from patients, we assumed that disruption of communication between T cells and myeloid cells by pharmacologic blockade of TNF and IFNγ could be a promising therapeutic strategy. Therefore, we compared the treatment effectiveness of TNF inhibitor or IL-6 inhibitor alone with combined blockade of TNF and IFNγ pathway (Fig. 6a, b). Both patients showed alleviation of fever frequencies and the inflammatory indexes. However, the P1 developed skin rashes during the treatment. Moreover, the increased serum levels of TNF in both patients could not be reversed by tocilizumab. The symptoms of colitis presented in P1 could not be relieved by tocilizumab (Fig. 6a). TNF-targeting therapy, adalimumab, was also administered, and both P1 and P2 responded with reduced severity of skin rashes and decreased frequency of fevers (Fig. 6a, b). Nevertheless, P2 still developed colitis (Fig. 6b). Moreover, adalimumab had limited effects on WBC and lymphocyte counts (Fig. 6c). At the same time, adalimumab alone was not enough to suppress serum levels of IL-6, in accordance with the partial inhibitory effect of adalimumab on IL-6 produced by MDMs in the co-culture assay (Fig. 6c and 5f). We next trailed the combined therapy blocking both TNF and IFNγ signaling in P1 and P2. Since the IFNγ-neutralizing antibody emapalumab was only approved for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis locally, we used ruxolitinib, which selectively targets IFNγ downstream JAK1/JAK2 kinase as an alternative in combination with adalimumab (Fig. 6a-c). Strikingly, after treated with combined therapy, both P1 and P2 no longer exhibited symptoms of fever and colitis and remained clinically asymptomatic for over one year. Concurrently, all tested inflammatory profiles, including increased counts and frequencies of WBC and lymphocyte, elevated serum levels of IL-6 and TNF, were recovered after the treatment (Fig. 6c). These results support a synergistic effect of TNF and IFN signaling in promoting the autoinflammation caused by RIPK1 activation-induced T cell death.

T cell death mediates autoinflammation in IECD

RIPK1 mutations at D324 3, 4 and SHARPIN deficiency 11, which could activate RIPK1 activation-induced cell death, have been reported to cause SAPIDs. Therefore, we examined the CD4/CD8 ratio and RIPK1 activation to verify our model. Similar to patients with RIPK1 K377E/R390G variants, we observed elevated CD4/CD8 ratio paired with increased RIPK1 phosphorylation and cleaved caspase-3 in PBMCs from CRIA patients (Fig. 7a-d, Supplementary Figure. 10a-c), indicating that CD8+ T cell death might be a general phenomenon during the inflammation of CRIA. Notably, CD8lo T cells from CRIA-1 and SHARPIN deficiency (Sharpenia) patients were increased upon in vitro culture (Fig.7e, f). CD4 and CD8 expression levels in CRIA patients’ T cells were validated by CyTOF and CD8 expression decreased more in CD8+ TEMRA cells than in other subsets, reflecting higher levels of cell death in CD8+ TEMRA cells (Supplementary Figure. 10d-f).

---

## Methods

Patients

Evaluation of the patients (P1 and P2; CRIA-1 and CRIA-2) was approved by Institutional Review Board and Ethical Committee at the Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital (2025-0440) and Children's Hospital (protocol 2021-IRB-172) of Zhejiang University School of Medicine. P1 and P2 were evaluated at Children’s Hospital affiliated to the Capital Institute of Pediatrics. SHARPIN deficiency patient were evaluated under the approval by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institutes of Health (94-HG-0105) as described30. All relevant ethical regulations were followed. All patients provided written informed consent.

Whole exome sequencing and genotyping with Sanger sequencing

Whole blood genomic DNA was extracted using Maxwell RSC Whole Blood DNA Kit (Promega, AS1520) and 1 μg DNA was used for whole-exome sequencing. WES and data analysis were performed as previously described31. For genotyping of other affected or unaffected family members, 437 bp genomic DNA fragment containing RIPK1 K377/R390 was amplified with forward primer 5’-TTGAGA TACAGATTCATGACGGCG-3’ and reverse primer 5’-CTGGTGCACTGCATTACCATGAC-3’ for Sanger sequencing. For genotyping of CRIA patients, 514 bp genomic DNA fragment containing RIPK1 D324 was amplified with forward primer 5’-AAATCAGGAAGTGTGAGTCCTACAACC-3’ and reverse primer 5’-TGTTCAGAACACTCTATGACTGGTGAG-3’ for Sanger sequencing.

Single-cell RNA sequencing

PBMCs of patient 1 and patient 2 were freshly isolated and 10000 single-cell were captured by 10X Genomics Chromium for cDNA library preparation according to the manufacturer’s instruction. Sequencing was carried out on Illumina NovaSeq PE150 platform by Novogene Company (Beijing, China). The resulting count matrices followed the standard pipeline with default parameters. Cell type annotation is based on reported annotation methods for PBMCs32, 33, 34, 35 and web-based databases like CellMarker36 and PanglaoDB37. Further data analysis was performed as previously described 31. NF-kB expression score and IFN response score of cell subtypes were calculated and the total cell number of each subtype from three unaffected controls or two patients, was employed for p-value calculations. Unaffected controls: CD14+ Mono, n=2915 cells; CD16+ Mono, n=398 cells; LDG, n=341 cells; pDC, n=108 cells; NK, n=1747 cells; CD4+ T, n=15028 cells; GZMK+ CD8+ T, n=2629 cells; GZMB+ CD8+ T, n=5272 cells; γδT, n=10 cells; Naive T, n=3678 cells; B, n=4535 cells; Plasma, n=87 cells. Patients: CD14+ Mono, n=4782 cells; CD16+ Mono, n=789 cells; LDG, n=11084 cells; pDC, n=139 cells; NK, n=1970 cells; CD4+ T, n=16463 cells; GZMK+ CD8+ T, n=2943 cells; GZMB+ CD8+ T, n=6124 cells; γδT, n=513 cells; Naive T, n=3779 cells; B, n=5586 cells; Plasma, n=159 cells.

Cell lines, cell isolation, culture and stimulation

The HEK293T and HT-29 cell lines were from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and were authenticated by STR profile report. Human PBMC samples were generated from peripheral blood samples using gradient centrifuging with LSM™ lymphocyte separation medium (MP Bio, Cat.50494X). Then primary T lymphocytes, primary CD8+/CD4+ T cells and monocytes were isolated from PBMCs by negative selection using Pan T Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-096-535), CD8+ T Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-096-495)/ CD4+ T Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-096-533) and Pan Monocyte Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-096-537) according to manufacturer’s instructions. SV40-HDFs were derived from skin biopsies of patient or control donors as described and transformed by lentiviral transduction of SV40-large T antigen. The HEK293T cells, SV40-HDFs were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS. Human PBMCs, primary T cells and monocytes were cultured in RPMI 1640 (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS. HT-29 cells were cultured in McCoy's 5A medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS.

Recombinant human TNF (Peprotech, 300-01A) was used to stimulate HT-29 cells (20 ng ml-1), SV40-HDFs (20 ng ml-1) and human primary monocytes (50 ng ml-1) for the indicated times. z-VAD-fmk (Selleck, S7023, 25 μM), SM-164 (Selleck, S7089, 250 nM) and Nec-1s (Selleck, S8641, 10 μM) were used to treat HT-29 cells, human primary T cells and monocytes. Staurosporine (MCE, HY-R15141, 100 nM) and RSL3 (Selleck, S8155, 1 μM) were used to induce apoptosis or ferroptosis in T cells.

Flow cytometry

Cells were washed with FACS buffer (0.5% BSA in PBS) and blocked with human Fc Block (BD Biosciences, 564219) or mouse Fc Block (BD Biosciences, 553141) followed by staining with antibodies against surface molecules in dark for 30 min at 4 °C. Then cells were washed twice and stained with Fixable Viability Stain 780 (BD Biosciences, 565388) to distinguish live versus dead cell. For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized with BD Phosflow Fix Buffer and Perm Buffer (BD Biosciences: 557870, 558052) and then washed twice and stained with antibodies against intracellular antigens for 30 min at 4 °C. For pRIPK1 (Ser166) and cleaved caspase-3 staining, cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor 647 labeled goat anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo, A-21244, 1:500) for 30 min at 4°C after primary antibody staining. Cells were acquired on CytoFlex (Beckman) and data were analyzed using FlowJo software. The following antibody clones were used for staining in flow cytometry analysis: CD3 (SK7, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), CD4 (RPA-T4, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), CD8 (RPA-T8, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), CD14 (M5E2, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), CD16 (3G8, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), CD19 (SJ25C1, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), CD56 (NCAM16.2, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), IL-1β (JK1B-1, BioLegend, 1: 100), TNF (MAb11, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), IL-6 (MQ2-13A5, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), IFNγ (4S.B3, BD Biosciences, 1: 100), Cleaved Caspase-3 (Asp175) (CST, #966S1, 1: 200), pRIPK1(Ser166, 1: 200) (D8I3A, CST), RIPK1 (D94C12, CST, 1: 800).

RNA isolation and real-time RT-PCR

Total RNA from cells was extracted using a RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, 74104) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 1 μg RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA with ReverTra Ace® qPCR RT Master Mix (TOYOTBO, FSQ-301). cDNA was then diluted and used for real-time PCR using 2x Universal SYBR Green Fast qPCR Mix (Abclonal, RK21203) with primers targeting IL1B (F, 5’-TGCTCTGGGATTCTCTTCAGC-3’; R, 5’-AAGTCATCCTCATTGCCACTGT-3’), IL6 (F, 5’-CATCCTCGACGGCATCTCAG-3’; R, 5’-ACCAGGCAAGTCTCCTCATTG-3’), IL8 (F 5’-CCAAACCTTTCCACCCCAAA-3’; R, 5’-GAATTCTCAGCCCTCTTCAAAAAC-3’) TNF (F, 5’-CTCTTCTGCCTGCTGCACTTTG-3’; R, 5’-ATGGGCTACAGGCTTGTCACTC-3’), and GAPDH (F, 5’-TCGACAGTCAGCCGCATCTTC-3’; R, 5’-GCGCCCAATACGACCAAATCC-3’). Relative transcription levels were calculated by normalization to GAPDH mRNA.

Cell viability assay and cell death assay

Primary T cells (15000 cells/well), SV40-HDFs (2000 cells/well) or HT-29 (5000 cells/well) were plated in 384-well plate and were stimulated with indicated conditions. General cell viability was measured by using CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega, G7572) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The percentage of viability was normalized to untreated controls. Cell death detection was performed by direct staining with 0.5 μg/ml Propidium Iodide (PI) and 0.5 μg/ml DAPI for 10 min and imaging with fluorescence microscope. PI positive dead cell was counted and normalized to DAPI counts. For continuous cell death measurement, cells were simulated with indicated conditions and stained with 200 nM Hoechst 33342 (Beyotime, C1022) and 200 nM SYTOX Orange (Thermo, S34861) at the same time. The percentage of dead cell was assayed every 1 hour by imaging with BioTek Cytation 3 for 18 hours with 5% CO and 37 °C condition. Results were exported as counts per well to be processed and graphed using Prism 9.

Protein array

Semiquantitative analysis of 174 cytokine levels of P2's serum samples before (normal stage) or after (onset, non-flare) the first onset of fever was performed with human Cytokine Array G2000 (RayBiotech) by Novogene Company (Beijing, China). Generally, the cytokine array glass slides were firstly blocked for 1 hour at room temperature and then incubated with 100 μl serum samples at 4 °C overnight. On the second day, the slides were washed with wash buffer and incubated with Biotin-Conjugated Anti-Cytokines and HiLyte Plus 555 Streptavidin-Fluor according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The results were scanned with InnoScan 300 Microarray Scanner (Innopsys) at 532 nm with 10 μm resolution. The mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was calculated and exported for further analysis. According to the pattern of serum cytokine changes corresponding to the fever stage, the differentially expressed cytokines compared with healthy donors were clustered into 3 groups as listed below. Group 1: GRO, MIF, uPAR, IL-12 p40, HGF, I-TAC, sTNF-RI, IL-11, ICAM-3, Eotaxin-2, IL-1 R4/ST2, IL-8, GCP-2, M-CSF, TRAIL R4, Osteoprotegerin, VEGF, MCP-3, IL-1β, FGF-4, MIP-3α, ENA-78, MIP-1α, TRAIL R3, MIP-1β, Lymphotactin. Group 2: MCP-2, ErbB3, IL-3, NT-4, Flt-3 Ligand, LAP, Dtk, b-NGF, IGFBP-1, MIP-3β, Fas/TNFRSF6, BLC, sTNF RII, Angiopoietin-2, IGFBP-3, IL-12 p70, IL-1α, IL-16, bFGF, TNF-α, MCP-4, LIF, MIG, IP-10. Group 3: HCC-4, Eotaxin, IGFBP-6, MPIF-1, DR6 (TNFRSF21), VEGF R3, IL-18 Rβ, Thrombopoietin, MMP-1, VE-Cadherin, PIGF, IL-2 Rγ, IL-1 R II, Leptin R, IL-18 BPα, IL-2 Rα, IL-2 Rβ, IL-4, PDGF Rβ, BMP-5, IL-13 Rα2, NGF R, Prolactin, Cardiotrophin-1, BMP-7, IL-10 Rβ, SDF-1β, IL-21R, IL-5 Rα, Siglec-5, TIMP-4, SCF.

Human and mouse cytokines measurement

Human or mouse serum cytokines were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Multi Sciences: 70-EK1280, 70-EK194, 70-EK182HS, 70-EK106HS, 70-EK191, 70-EK180HS, 70-EK1F01, 70-EK1F02, EK206HS, EK282HS/2) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. T cell culture supernatant cytokines were determined by Cytometric Bead Arrays (BD Biosciences) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Human serum adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity was measured with Boyle colorimetric method by using ADA Activity Assay Kit (Yuanye Bio, R22207) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Student’s t-test was performed for the statistical analysis.

In vitro cell proliferation assay

Fresh isolated CD3+ T cells were labeled with CFSE (Thermo, 65-0850-84, 5 μM) and then stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 beads (T&L Biotechnology) at 1:1 ratio supplemented with hrIL-7 (PrimeGene) and hrIL-15 (PrimeGene) in 48-well plates for 96 hours. Then all cells were co-stained with CD4-BB515 and CD8-BV510 antibodies and analyzed using CytoFlex (Beckman).

Gene editing of patient T cells

Primary T cells isolated from patients were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 beads for 3 days. For electroporation, 180 pmol sgRNA and 25 μg Cas9 protein were mixed and incubated for 15 min at room temperature for ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNP) formation. Then 3e6 T cells resuspended in opti-MEM were mixed with RNP and 6 μg dsDNA template and electroporated using Gemini X2 (BTX) under the #905 program for human primary T cells. After electroporation, 1 ml warm X-VIVOTM 15 Serum-free Hematopoietic Cell Medium (Lonza) supplemented with 10% FBS was immediately added to the cuvette and the mixture was then carefully transferred to 24-well plates for further culture and analysis.

T cell-MDM co-culture assay

Freshly isolated monocytes were seeded in 24-well plate and differentiated into MDMs with 20 ng/ml GM-CSF treatment for 10 days. Then, 0.4 µm pore polycarbonate membrane inserts containing T cells isolated from PBMCs of patient or healthy donors were placed into the 24-well plate for the T cell-MDM co-culture at the ratio of 5:1 for 8 hours. Finally, T cells were removed and bottom MDMs were collected for mRNA extraction.

Mice

All mouse studies complied with relevant ethical regulations and approved by Laboratory Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee of Zhejiang University (Registration No.: ZJU20230495). The Cd8-creERT2 and Lyz2-creERT2 strains on C57BL/6J background were purchased from GemPharmatech. The Rosa26-mTmG strain on C57BL/6J background was purchased from Cyagen. The Ripk1 knockout and Ripk1 +/k376r mouse strains were kind gifts from Professor Haibing Zhang (Shanghai Institute of Nutrition and Health, , Chinese Academy of Sciences). All mice were maintained under specific pathogen-free condition with free access to food and water at Laboratory Animal Center of Zhejiang University (Temperature: 20–26℃, humidity: 40–70%, light intensity: 15–20 lx, noise: <60 dB). In mouse studies, male Rosa26-mTmG mice in lineage negative bone marrow cell transplantation assay were used. For other mouse strains, mice were randomized assigned to the experiments with no regard for sex.

Lineage negative bone marrow cells isolation, transduction, transplantation, induction and LPS challenge

Mice were euthanized by CO₂ inhalation. Mouse lineage negative bone marrow cells (Lin– BMs, including hematopoietic stem cells and marrow stromal cells) from bone marrow were isolated from 6- to 8-week-old donor mice using Lineage cell depletion kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-090-858) according to manufacturer’s instruction. Lin– BMs were plated in 12-well plate and were transduced with lentivirus carrying human RIPK1 inducible expression system (MOI=50). Transduction efficiencies were measured with flow cytometry after 24 hours culturing and 200,000 of transduced Lin– BMs cells were transplanted into lethally irradiated (4 Gy, 2 times) male recipient mice (8 to 12 weeks old). Transplantation efficiencies were validated by flow cytometry analysis after 2 weeks. Successfully transplanted mice were injected i.p with 20 mg/ml tamoxifen (MCE, HY-13757A) dissolved in corn oil (MCE, HY-Y1888) every two days for 5 times to induce the expression of WT, K377E, R390G or D324V mutated RIPK1. Then, these mice were injected i.p with 0.5 mg/kg lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Sigma, L6529) and serum were collected before injection or injected for 2 hours. Serum Il6 and Tnf were measured by ELISA as described.

Immunoprecipitation and western blot

For TNFR signaling complex (TNF-RSC) enrichment, 5e6 SV40-HDF cells or HT-29 cells were seeded and treated with flag tagged TNF (ENZO, ALX-522-008) for indicated times. The samples were immediately washed with cold PBS and lysed in cold lysis buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 10% glycerol) with freshly added inhibitors blocking protease and phosphatase (Merck: 4906837001, 4693159001) for 30 min. Then samples were cleared through centrifugation at 20000 xg for 10 min and protein concentrations were determined by Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kits (Thermo, 23225). Then the TNF-RSC was immunoprecipitated with FLAG M2 magnetic beads (Sigma, M8823) at 4 °C for 4 hours and the protein complex was directly eluted by boiling in 1×SDS loading buffer. For TNF downstream signaling analysis, 4e5 cells were seeded and treated as indicated and then cells were harvested and lysed directly with sample loading buffer. These samples were separated through routine SDS-PAGE and transferred to 0.45 μm nitrocellulose membrane (Cytiva, 10600002) and blotted with indicated antibodies (For Western blotting, antibodies were applied at a 1:1000 dilution).

CyTOF

PBMCs were freshly isolated from whole bloods of four patients (P1 and P2; CRIA-1 and CRIA-2) and four unaffected controls, then blocked and labeled with conjugated antibodies as described38. Fixed cell samples were resuspend analyzed on a mass cytometer (Helios, Fluidigm). The CyTOF data exported as FCS files were gated in FlowJo (v10.0.7) to remove doublets and CD45+ single cells identified by DNA (191Ir and 193Ir)、194Pt and event length. For downstream analysis, 10,000 cells were randomly selected from each sample. The raw values of FCS files were transformed using the arcsinh function with a cofactor of 5. Phenograph clustering in cytofkit R package was performed on all subsampled sample events and the transformed values of all events were subjected to t-SNE dimension reduction using R-tsne package39, 40.

Antibodies

The following antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology: pRIPK1 (S166) (65746), RIPK1 (3493), pMLKL (S358) (91689), MLKL (14993), pIKKα/β (S176/180) (2697), IKKβ (2370), Sharpin (12541), pp65 (S65) (3033), p65 (8242), pIκBα (S32) (2859), IκBα (4814), pERK1/2 (T202/Υ204) (4370), ERK1/2 (4695), pJNK (T183/Y185) (9251), JNK (9252), HA (3724), cleaved caspase-3 (D175) (9661), caspase-3 (9662). NEMO (sc-8330) was purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology. GAPDH (SA30-01) was purchased from HUABIO.

Data availability

The raw sequence data of single-cell RNA sequencing generated in this study have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive in National Genomics Data Center, China National Center for Bioinformation/Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (GSA-Human) under accession code: HRA016329 [https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/browse/HRA016329]. The raw whole-exome sequencing data are protected and are not publicly available due to data privacy laws and ethnics policy. Due to patient privacy concerns, the data generated from human samples can be obtained from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. All other study data are available within the article or its supplementary information files with no restriction or from the corresponding author. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors make a compelling case for primary CD8 T-cells as sensitised for (RIPK1 induced) programmed cell death as instigators for triggering an elevated inflammatory response of autologous monocytes in patients with inherited inborn errors of cell death. Patient data (of 2 siblings) and mouse model data piece together a story that includes genetic reconstitution data, additional CRIA patient family data and is confirmed by anti-TNF/IFN treatment data of the patients. This reviewer is overall satisfied by the wealth of data presented. However, could it be that other cells, non-immune cells such as smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells and fibroblasts that can produce TNF, contribute to the auto inflammatory disease? It might not only CD8+ T-cells that instigate the cascade; perhaps TNF produced by tissue cells (non-immune cells) triggers the auto inflammatory cascade that otherwise works via increased sensitisation to apoptosis. please comment. Otherwise, only small points, a graphic summary would be a helpful addition to the manuscript (although the journal editors should decide if this fits). Two typographical errors seen in line 293 (generated) and 357 (specially).

### Reviewer 2

Dai et al have identified two related autoinflammatory disease patients with heterozygous variants in RIPK1 K377E/R390G. They associate these heterozygous variants with increased CD8+ T cell death and elevated inflammatory cytokine secretion from patient monocytes and macrophages. Disruption of crosstalk between CD8+ T cells and myeloid cells by pharmacological inhibition of TNF and JAK1/2 resulted in disease control. This is a noteworthy study which would be of interest to the rare disease community. The characterisation of individual cell types (T cells, monocytes, etc), their interactions and the proposed mechanism of how this drives disease is extensive and well executed, particularly use of the transwell culture system and HSCs-transplantation in Figure 5. However, the mechanistic insight into how the R390G variant contributes to disease is lacking and a cause for concern. Because this is a study on a single kindred to convincingly show that this is a monogenic disorder the authors should correct the patient mutations in patient cells (eg: fibroblasts) using homology directed repair or prime editing. Then determine NFkB signalling and cell death responses to TNF stimulation. These isogenic cells would be ideal controls in all follow up experiments. Disruption of the ubiquitination site: K377 through a missense substitution to an E is understandably pathogenic, RIPK1 ubiquitination at K377 is required for stable TNFR induced NFkB activation rather than TNFR triggered cell death (PMID: 16603398, PMID: 16543241, PMID: 32999468). Over expression of K377E RIPK1 in HT-29 cells shows a convincing increased phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL and decrease in NFkB signalling, ubiquitination of and elevated cell death, in response to TNF stimulation (Ex Fig 2), although these should be quantified and the appropriate number of experimental replications (ie: at least three) should be performed. These data, coupled with the induction of elevated NFkB driven cytokines in serum of mice transplanted with K377E RIPK1 T cells (Figure 5) provide a solid argument for K377E RIPK1 driving disease. In contrast, R390G RIPK1 expression alone had a limited effect on RIPK1 and MLKL phosphorylation and NFKB signalling in response to TNF stimulation (Ex data 2i and g). This data is particularly unconvincing since it is representative of only two replicates. At a minimum these experiments should be performed three times and densitometry changes for relevant bands should be presented (eg: (p)p65 compared to p65, IkBa bands relative to zero time point of each cell line, etc). Similarly, the change in TNFa and IL-6 in mouse serum in R390G RIPK1 expressing CD8+ linage cells is modest compared to WT RIPK1 expressing cells and it appears that this experiment has only been performed once. R390G RIPK1 overexpression does associate with increased TNF induced cell death in HT-29s (Ex Fig 2e-f) and R390G RIPK1 ubiquitination does appear delayed in Ex Fig 2l). But the data presented to validate the author’s proposed mechanism of R390G driving dysfunction of RIPK1 via interrupting interaction with MIB2 (Ex Fig 2l-n) is not convincing. Ubiquitination of WT and R390G RIPK1 looks comparable to me in Ex Fig 2m and the change in MIB2 binding in minimal in Ex Fig 2n and could be explained by the slightly smaller pulled down FLAG band (again, quantification using densitometry would help with data interpretation). The authors also do not provide reasoning on how a change to a glycine at 390 would interrupt binding to MIB2. Overall, I am not convinced that R390G RIPK1is a disease driving variant in itself, it may instead be a disease modifying variant that is only pathogenic in the context of a driving variant such as K377E. eg: R390G RIPK1 could have decreased stability and is not/lowly expressed in patient cells (this may not be seen in an over expression system), therefore disease pathogenesis is driven almost entirely driven by K377E. I note that while the CADD score is high, alpha missense rates this amino acid change for R390G as “ambiguous”. I encourage the authors to better determine the effect of R390G to publish the most robust findings which clinicians may take advice from. Here are a few points the authors should address to determine the role of R390G RIPK1: 1. Stability of R390G RIPK1: Use the established HT-29 over expression system to perform a cycloheximide chase to compare stability of R390G RIPK1 with other RIPK1 variants. 2. Interaction with MIB2: Try titrating levels of RIPK1 variants and/or MIB2 in the over expression IP to clearly show a decreased interaction between MIB2 and R390G over a range of concentrations. Alternatively, try BioID or TurboID. 3. Determine if Ubiquitination of RIPK1 at 377 is altered: Given that in the patient cells RIPK1 Ub is altered post TNF stimulation but the R390G mutant looks comparable to WT (over expression) it may be that (if stable) R390G inhibits K377 ubiquitination but does not affect other Ub sites on RIPK1. Thus, the change in Ub could be masked in the over expression system. The authors should specifically determine if K377 Ub is altered, eg: using plasmid mutagenesis to isolate specific Ub sites on RIPK1 and compare WT to R390G or perform Ub site mapping by Mass Spec. 4. Could R390G disrupt RIPK1 interaction with proteins other than MIB2 which are important for recruitment to the TNFR1 cytoplasmic domain or ubiquitination eg: TRADD (PMID: 8612133), cIAPs (PMID: 25192652) this could be tested in the same over expression system as Ex Data Fig 2. 5. The authors should also determine if R390 effects: RIPK1 trafficking to the TNFR1 complex, confirmational changes that allow RIPK1 to interact with other proteins or alters dimerization. I recommend the authors also try testing the above with coexpression of R390G with WT or K377E RIPK1 as this may contribute to the phenotype. Discussion Points that should be included: The authors should contextualise their findings on the T cell/Mono Mac driven disease course in autoinflammatory disorders driven by RIPK1 variants with autoinflammatory diseases driven by OTULIN deficiency/dysfuncton(driven almost entirely by myeloid cells, PMID: 30804083) and LUBAC deficient patients (more involvement of lymphocytes and stromal cell types, eg: PMID: 32687504, PMID: 31462647, PMID: 35534698, etc) The equivocation of monoclonal blockade of IFNg in Figure 5f and treatment of patients with ruxolitinib (Fig 6) is incorrect, JAK1/2 blockade inhibits inflammatory signalling from a variety of cytokines including IFNab and IL-6 which are elevated in the RIPK1 patients. I appreciate that the authors call this treatment regime TNF/IFN but the distinction should be highlighted in the discussion. Particularly because RIPK1 has been shown to drive IFNab signalling under conditions of OTULIN dysfuncton(PMID: 29950720) and JAK1/2 blockade had therapeutic benefit in these patients (PMC11022884 ). Do the authors think that IFNg is specifically is important for cell death in these patients as per PMID: 35139355? -No increase in TSZ induced cell death compared to TS and TZ, in fact TSZ looked less effective than TS in T cells (Figure 1h) -comment? Minor Points: The manuscript presents an impressive amount of experimental data; but many key experiments have been performed only once or twice (from my reading of the legends) and generally only show a single representative repeat. As I highlighted in the context of western blotting of the NFkB signalling cascade this is a real problem when trying to establish the robustness of the patient phenotype. This is particularly important to the field of rare disease since these findings may be used for differential diagnosis of other patients, reporting that there is a strong effect when it is actually variable will impede our understanding of other novel RIPK1 variants. The authors need to repeat key experiments at least three times to strengthen the validity of their conclusions and provide summary data from independent biological replicates (ie: pooling results across experiments). -Ex Figure 2A is missing panels and does not appear to show protection from cell death by Nec-1 in patient fibroblasts. Please quantify to clearly show this result. -Ext Fig 3e, panels are missing -Extended 2d,e should have empty vector control -No isotype controls shown for Fig 2f -Please list for cytokine groups in Figure 3. “which was reported to induce more severer cell death in Ripk1K376R/K376R cells” Should say: “which was reported to induce more sever cell death …"

### Reviewer 3

Biallelic loss-of-functon(LOF) variants in RIPK1 cause RIPK1 deficiency, whereas monoallelic cleavage-resistant gain-of-functon(GOF) variants result in an autoinflammatory syndrome called cleavage-resistant RIPK1 induced autoinflammatory (CRIA) syndrome. In this manuscript, Jialin Dai, Qing Zhou, and colleagues describe two patients from a single family harboring compound heterozygous missense variants in RIPK1 (K377E and R390G), who presented with an autoinflammatory syndrome characterized by recurrent fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, and enteropathy. At the molecular level, the RIPK1-K377E variant was shown to be ubiquitination-deficient and constitutively active. The R390G variant is also considered a GOF mutation, although concerns remain regarding its pathogenicity and molecular mechanism, as discussed in major comment no. 4. Functional studies demonstrated augmented apoptosis and necroptosis following TNF stimulation in the patients’ dermal fibroblasts and primary T cells, consistent with RIPK1 GOF activity. scRNA-seq of patients’ PBMCs identified an aberrant monocyte/macrophage population with elevated proinflammatory cytokine expression. CyTOF-based PBMC subset analysis revealed reduced frequencies of CD8+ T cells in the patients. Upon anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation in in vitro, a further decrease in CD8-hi T cells and an emergence of CD8-lo T cells were noted. Cytokine production was enhanced in both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells. Co-culture experiments with patient-derived T cells and healthy donor monocyte-derived macrophages demonstrated that the patient T cells exacerbated proinflammatory cytokine production by allogeneic monocyte-derived macrophages, suggesting a central role of T cells in driving autoinflammation in these patients. Therapeutically, the patients’ autoinflammatory manifestations were successfully managed with the anti-TNFα monoclonal antibody adalimumab and the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib. Notably, a reduced proportion of CD8+ T cells among total T cells was also consistently observed in other immune dysregulation conditions, including CRIA and SHARPIN deficiency. In summary, the experiments in this study are thoughtfully designed, and the data generated are largely robust and support the central conclusions. However, several experiments require revision or clarification, as detailed in the major and minor comments below. This study demonstrate decreased CD8+ T cells as one of common immunological abnormalities in other inborn errors of cell death (IECD) such as CRIA and SHARPIN deficiency, indicating the CD8+ T cell-driven autoinflammation may play a role in other IECDs. While this study will likely be of interest to researchers in the field of inborn errors of immunity, the findings may limit its appeal to the broader readership of Nature Communications. I believe the manuscript may be more appropriately suited for a clinically oriented journal that emphasizes translational research and patient-centered findings. Major comments: 1. One of the study’s principal observations is the pronounced depletion of CD8+ T cells in patients carrying RIPK1‑K377E/R390G variants and, similarly, in those with CRIA. The authors hypothesize that augmented programmed cell death of CD8+ T cells results in increased cytokine release from those cells, in turn, potentiate monocytes and macrophages to secrete proinflammatory cytokines. To support this model, direct comparisons of CD8+ versus CD4+ T cell responses are indispensable. Several critical comparisons, however, are currently missing: - Viability following TS or TSZ stimulation (as shown in Fig 1h) for CD8+ versus CD4+ T cells - Phosphorylation of MLKL (as shown in Extended Data Fig 2c) in CD8+ versus CD4+ T cells - Proliferation following anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation (as shown in Fig 4b) for CD8+ versus CD4+ T cells 2. Disruption of the ubiquitination site: K377 through a missense substitution to an E is
understandably pathogenic, RIPK1 ubiquitination at K377 is required for stable TNFR induced
NFkB activation rather than TNFR triggered cell death (PMID: 16603398, PMID: 16543241,

elevated cell death, in response to TNF stimulation (Ex Fig 2), although these should be quantified
